title: Show like a pro

slides.title: Show like a pro
slides.lead: Day 3 · A 75-minute live workshop
slides.body: Help the buyer understand what works, what does not, and what to do next.
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-property
slides.notes:
Today we are going to work on the first showing. Success is not whether they buy the house we open. Success is whether we understand them better and they leave knowing how we will help them move forward. Introduce yourself and connect today to the first-call work in Day 2.
Handoff: Let’s walk through the visit in the same order you will experience it with a buyer.
Sources: INT-005–007; Eric’s Day 3 objective. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Let’s walk through the visit in the same order you will experience it with a buyer.

slides.title: From a first meeting to a useful plan
slides.lead: We will learn the approach, discuss the difficult moments, then practice the full conversation.
slides.body:
Before the visit

Prepare useful comparisons and set expectations.

At the home

Give the buyer room to react, then understand those reactions.

Before you leave

Connect priorities, concerns, and timing to an agreed plan.

Practice together

Take turns as agent, buyer, and observer. Give feedback and retry.
slides.notes:
Explain that discussion is part of the lesson. Ask for the reasoning behind answers, including what information would change someone’s recommendation. People with HQ submit on the question slide. People without HQ can answer aloud; choose the group’s multiple-choice answer in your presenter window and submit it to discuss. Open private presenter notes in their own tab and share only the presentation window.
Handoff: The plan starts before we arrive: why are we showing these particular homes?
Sources: INT-015; INT-037–039; user training preferences. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: The plan starts before we arrive: why are we showing these particular homes?

slides.title: Give each home a reason to be on the tour
slides.lead: Use what the buyer told you to propose two or three useful comparisons.
slides.body:
Connect to a need

“You wanted room to work from home. This one has an enclosed office.”

Name the tradeoff

“The yard is smaller than you asked for. Would comparing the layout still be useful?”

Confirm the visit

Check access, showing instructions, the meeting plan, and the applicable brokerage-approved agreement.
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-home
slides.notes:
Explain why multiple homes help: the buyer can compare, priorities become clearer, and one unavailable home need not end the outing. A comparison is not permission to ignore criteria. Tell them where it differs and why you are suggesting it. Respect their time and decision. Confirm the actual form and access; do not promise universal agreement terms or treat a requested time as confirmed access.
Handoff: Once the plan is clear, the way we welcome them determines how comfortable they feel being honest.
Sources: R012; R016; R018; R021; INT-015,037–039. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Once the plan is clear, the way we welcome them determines how comfortable they feel being honest.

slides.title: Make it safe to dislike the home
slides.lead: “Drop the rope” means the buyer can be honest without having to defend their reaction.
slides.body: “I’m excited to show you around. You do not have to make this home work. Tell me what you like and what you would change. That helps us figure out what to look for next.”
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-arrival
slides.notes:
Demonstrate this as a normal welcome, not a memorized speech. Explain that the goal is to help them find the right fit, whether this home works or the search takes longer. Follow through: if they criticize the kitchen, get curious instead of defending it. Invite someone to describe what an agent could do later that would contradict this welcome.
Handoff: Let’s put that promise to a test: what happens when your suggested comparison feels wrong to the buyer?
Sources: Repository SALES_DOCTRINE: Drop the rope; R021; INT-038–039. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Let’s put that promise to a test: what happens when your suggested comparison feels wrong to the buyer?

slides.title: “That is not what we asked for.”
slides.lead: A buyer wants a home office and a large yard. Your suggested home has an office but a small yard. They say, “You are not listening.” What is your best next move? Explain why.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example
Start with B. Acknowledge the mismatch and learn what the yard needs to do for them. Explain the comparison only if it is useful, then narrow the search if that is their preference. A and C may eventually help, but each assumes the solution before understanding the reaction.
slides.notes:
Give everyone thirty seconds to choose and submit. Hear two different reasons before sharing the example. Ask: What could you have said before adding this home to the tour? What changes if the buyer has already said the yard is nonnegotiable? The point is to understand their priority, not win approval for your pick.
Handoff: Now we have a useful tour plan. Inside the home, the challenge is knowing when to speak and when to give them space.
Sources: R021; INT-038–039. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Now we have a useful tour plan. Inside the home, the challenge is knowing when to speak and when to give them space.

activity.prompt: A buyer wants a home office and a large yard. Your suggested home has an office but a small yard. They say, “You are not listening.” What is your best next move? Explain why.

fields.label: Explain your choice. What would change if the yard were nonnegotiable?

activity.model: Start with B. Acknowledge the mismatch and learn what the yard needs to do for them. Explain the comparison only if it is useful, then narrow the search if that is their preference. A and C may eventually help, but each assumes the solution before understanding the reaction.

choices.text: Explain why the office makes this home worth seeing and finish the tour.
Acknowledge the mismatch and ask what they need from the yard before revising the plan.
Replace it with the largest-yard home in the search and keep the appointment time.

activity.explanation: Start with B. Acknowledge the mismatch and learn what the yard needs to do for them. Explain the comparison only if it is useful, then narrow the search if that is their preference. A and C may eventually help, but each assumes the solution before understanding the reaction.

slides.title: Let them experience the home
slides.lead: Stay available, notice their reactions, and contribute information that helps them decide.
slides.body:
Give them room

Let the buyer look and talk. You do not need to narrate every room.

Follow their reaction

“You paused in the office. What were you picturing using it for?”

Separate fact from guess

If a property question is unresolved, say so and explain how you will seek the answer.
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-conversation
slides.notes:
Demonstrate a short silence while the buyer looks around, then a question based on something they actually said. Do not read a facial expression as a conclusion. Being quiet is not disappearing: be available and answer useful questions. Preserve the existing showing teaching about giving space. Tie factual uncertainty to Eric’s problem-solving rule: prepare a useful next step, not a guessed answer.
Handoff: Being helpful gets harder when two buyers react differently to the same space.
Sources: Existing Day 3 showing conduct; R002; R025. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Being helpful gets harder when two buyers react differently to the same space.

slides.title: Questions that make the next home a better fit
slides.lead: Choose a question that follows the buyer’s answer. You do not need to ask the whole list.
slides.body:
Understand the use

“How would you use this space?” · “What is difficult about your current setup?”

Find the difference

“What worked better in the other home?” · “What made this one feel different in person?”

Explore priorities

“Which part would you miss most?” · “What would make that tradeoff worth considering?”

Check your understanding

“So a separate workspace matters more than an extra bedroom—is that right?”
slides.notes:
Give agents this as a working question bank, not a checklist. Model asking one question, listening, and building the next question from the answer. “A bigger house” becomes useful when we learn why the current space fails. A summary is a check with the buyer, not an agent deciding their priorities for them.
Handoff: Use those questions in this situation. We need to understand both buyers before suggesting a compromise.
Sources: R005; R021; INT-005–007,038. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Use those questions in this situation. We need to understand both buyers before suggesting a compromise.

slides.title: One home. Two different reactions.
slides.lead: During a first tour, one buyer loves the open living area. Their partner says, “I could never work from home here.” What would you do first, and why?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example
B gives both people room to explain. Learn what “work from home” requires before proposing a physical fix or changing the search. A might become useful after verification and buyer interest; C might fit after both buyers agree on the priority.
slides.notes:
Ask agents to choose, then explain what each answer would help them learn and what it could miss. After reveal, invite two volunteers to play the buyers. Give them one sentence each about a workday and have an agent ask a responsive follow-up. Do not turn this into settling a disagreement for the couple.
Handoff: Those observations give us something useful to talk about when the tour ends. Here is how to open that conversation.
Sources: R005; R021; derived practice case. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Those observations give us something useful to talk about when the tour ends. Here is how to open that conversation.

fields.label: Explain your choice. What would you need to hear from each buyer?

activity.model: B gives both people room to explain. Learn what “work from home” requires before proposing a physical fix or changing the search. A might become useful after verification and buyer interest; C might fit after both buyers agree on the priority.

choices.text: Explore whether the dining area could become a workspace.
Ask each buyer how they would use the home during a normal day.
Suggest making an enclosed office a required search filter.

activity.explanation: B gives both people room to explain. Learn what “work from home” requires before proposing a physical fix or changing the search. A might become useful after verification and buyer interest; C might fit after both buyers agree on the priority.

slides.title: Ask for a few minutes before they leave
slides.lead: Make the purpose clear: use today’s reactions to decide what would help next.
slides.body: “Thanks for being honest about the house. Do you have a couple of minutes? I’d like to understand what worked and what didn’t so we can make the next step useful for you.”
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-coaching
slides.notes:
This adapts Eric’s opening in INT-005. He asks for time and explains the purpose before asking questions. Then ask whether any home is worth exploring further. If none, learn what was missing. If they are rushed, agree on another useful time rather than force a parking-lot consultation. Demonstrate a calm transition from the tour to this conversation.
Handoff: Let’s watch how a specific answer changes the next question.
Sources: R005; INT-005. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Let’s watch how a specific answer changes the next question.

slides.title: “The kitchen and yard did not work.”
slides.lead: Fictional example: the buyer rejects the first home. The agent uses that answer to learn what a better fit would look like.
slides.body:
Buyer

“The kitchen felt dated, and the yard was too small.”

Agent

“What do you need the yard to let you do?”

Buyer

“We want room for our two dogs to run. We do not want a renovation project.”

Agent

“If the yard worked and the kitchen was ready to use, how close would that get us? What else would still be missing?”
slides.notes:
Read this exchange with a volunteer. Explain Eric’s hypothetical rating approach: imagine the named problems addressed, then ask how close the home would be and why. You can use a one-to-ten rating, but the number is a conversation starter. An imagined improved home is not this home, and a high rating is not permission to write an offer. Ask what we now know that “they did not like it” would have missed.
Handoff: Sometimes the answer shows that a different property will not solve the whole concern.
Sources: R002; R005; INT-005–006. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Sometimes the answer shows that a different property will not solve the whole concern.

slides.title: Acknowledge. Understand. Offer useful help.
slides.lead: A concern deserves both empathy and a response that fits the reason behind it.
slides.body:
Acknowledge

“I can understand why feeling tied down would give you pause.”

Ask to understand

“What would you want to keep flexible? What drew you to looking at homes now?”

Offer a solution

Use their answer to propose useful information, a comparison, a next conversation, or a plan to wait.
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-concern
slides.notes:
Present the framework before the next discussion. Eric’s point is that immediate agreement can leave the buyer’s concern untouched, while pushing toward a predetermined purchase also fails them. Ask questions because their reasons matter. Education and a recommendation follow understanding. Waiting can be the right recommendation. Do not make promises about future prices, rates, or investment safety.
Handoff: Now try it with a buyer whose hesitation may be about ownership itself.
Sources: R006; R024; INT-007,045–050. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Now try it with a buyer whose hesitation may be about ownership itself.

slides.title: “Renting gives us flexibility.”
slides.lead: After the tour, the buyer says, “Even if the house were perfect, I am not sure I want to own. Renting gives us flexibility.” What would you ask before recommending anything?
slides.body:
Discuss what different answers might mean. Then describe how your recommendation would change.

Compare with the teaching example
“That makes sense. What flexibility is important to you, and what prompted you to look at buying?” Listen. A possible relocation may call for planning around uncertainty; a monthly-cost concern may call for information from a lender. These are examples, not facts about this buyer. Agree on help that fits, including waiting.
slides.notes:
Give thirty seconds to write, then take several responses. Push beyond repeating “why?” Ask one agent to supply a possible buyer answer and another to respond to that answer. Compare a temporary work assignment with uncertainty about monthly costs. Neither reason is established by the original statement. Do not grade the room on persuading the buyer to buy. Look for an acknowledgment, a useful question, and a recommendation that changes with the answer.
Handoff: Once we understand what is behind the hesitation, we can discuss preparation and timing without making the buyer feel screened.
Sources: R006; R024; INT-007,045–050. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Once we understand what is behind the hesitation, we can discuss preparation and timing without making the buyer feel screened.

activity.prompt: After the tour, the buyer says, “Even if the house were perfect, I am not sure I want to own. Renting gives us flexibility.” What would you ask before recommending anything?

fields.label: Write your acknowledgment and the question you would ask.
Give two possible buyer answers. How would each change your recommendation?

activity.model: “That makes sense. What flexibility is important to you, and what prompted you to look at buying?” Listen. A possible relocation may call for planning around uncertainty; a monthly-cost concern may call for information from a lender. These are examples, not facts about this buyer. Agree on help that fits, including waiting.

slides.title: Make preparation relevant to their situation
slides.lead: The usual time to introduce financing is when the buyer raises it or at the end of the first showing.
slides.body:
Start with the goal

“If we find a home that fits, would you be using financing? Have you worked with a lender already?”

Learn the timing

“What is driving that timeframe?” · “What needs to happen before you can move?”

Connect the help

“Would it help to understand the payment range before we choose the next homes?”
slides.notes:
Explain that financing is not a test of whether they deserved today’s showing. Connect it to what the buyer wants to understand. Ask about their existing lender relationship before offering an introduction. Do not quote products, approval outcomes, or credit effects you have not verified. A buyer a year out may still benefit from planning now if affordability or credit uncertainty explains the delay. A lease end is a fact to explore, not proof of a purchase deadline.
Handoff: Let me show you how those answers become a plan the buyer can actually use.
Sources: R001–004; R020; R024; INT-003–005,050. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Let me show you how those answers become a plan the buyer can actually use.

slides.title: Turn the answers into an agreement
slides.lead: Fictional example: the buyer needs a usable yard, wants no renovation, and is deciding whether to buy before a lease ends in four months.
slides.body: “We’ll focus on move-in-ready homes with room for the dogs. You’d like payment information before deciding whether buying fits. With your permission, I’ll introduce you to a lender today. You’ll choose a time to talk, and we’ll reconnect Tuesday at 6 to decide what makes sense next. Does that plan work for you?”
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-questions
slides.notes:
Explain that every fact here came from the fictional conversation; do not supply those facts for a real buyer. Model listening to whether Tuesday works and changing it if needed. An introduction is an offered action until the buyer accepts it, not a completed lender conversation. The plan needs a purpose, who will do what, and an agreed next contact. Do not turn four months into an order to buy.
Handoff: A good plan also needs to hold up when one important answer is still missing.
Sources: R005; R020–021; INT-005,035–037. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: A good plan also needs to hold up when one important answer is still missing.

slides.title: The buyer is interested. The answer is missing.
slides.lead: After a showing, a buyer says they may want to make an offer, but need the roof age first. You promised an update by 5. It is 4:45, and the listing agent has not replied. What would you do next?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example
B fits the uncertainty. Keep the buyer informed before five, clarify how the answer affects their decision, and seek team-lead advice if it is urgent. Propose a next update you control. Do not guarantee a third-party answer. A may become appropriate after agreement and understanding urgency; C assumes enough information to set an offer plan.
slides.notes:
Ask for a choice and the information that could change it. Discuss the difference between “I may want to offer” and “I need this now to decide on an offer.” Ask: What can you commit to when you cannot control the listing agent? What should the buyer hear by five? Have an agent speak the update. Reveal the example after the room has worked through the tradeoff.
Handoff: Whether we are waiting on an answer or planning another tour, the buyer should know what happens next.
Sources: R025; INT-051. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Whether we are waiting on an answer or planning another tour, the buyer should know what happens next.

slides.title: Can the buyer explain the plan back to you?
slides.lead: A useful next step answers these questions in plain English.
slides.body:
Why this step?

What did we learn today, and what question or need does this address?

Who does what?

What will you do? What has the buyer agreed to do? What remains unresolved?

When do we reconnect?

Agree on a time or a clear trigger and a useful way to communicate.
slides.notes:
Compare “I will send you listings” with “I will send two options with enclosed offices tonight; we will talk Wednesday at six about whether either is worth touring.” The exact plan depends on the buyer. For someone waiting, agree on what information would help and how to stay in touch. Ask them to confirm or adjust the plan. Respect a decision not to continue. Do not manufacture a date just to fill a field.
Handoff: Your record should preserve the same plan, so follow-through does not depend on memory.
Sources: R020–021; R024; INT-035–039,050. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Your record should preserve the same plan, so follow-through does not depend on memory.

slides.title: Save what changed and what you promised
slides.lead: The next contact should have a valid business reason connected to this buyer.
slides.body:
Factual note

Record what worked, what did not, the reason for timing, and the agreed plan. Keep unknowns unknown.

Correct stage

Use Met with customer after the first appointment; Showing homes after the second.

Follow-through

Use a dated FUB task to support the agreed action. Deliver the update even if an outside answer is still pending.
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-follow-up
slides.notes:
Connect this to Day 1 without reteaching the whole record. An honest comparison update can be useful even when no home matches perfectly. Explain why it is relevant and honor the communication preference. A task is a reminder; completing it is not evidence that the buyer accepted a new plan. Next we practice the whole conversation and then write the record from what was actually said.
Handoff: You now have the pieces. Let’s put them together with a buyer who can answer back.
Sources: R021; R025; existing Day 1 stage definitions. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: You now have the pieces. Let’s put them together with a buyer who can answer back.

slides.title: Conduct the visit. Leave with a plan.
slides.lead: Work in pairs or trios. Everyone takes an agent turn and responds to what the buyer actually says.
slides.body:
Set up · 1 minute

Choose the assigned buyer card. Use the meeting platform for breakout rooms.

Three rounds · 4 minutes each

Agent: welcome and discovery for 2 minutes. Observer: one specific correction for 1 minute. Agent: retry for 1 minute. Rotate roles.

Debrief · 3 minutes

What answer changed your plan? What did your partner improve on the retry?

Compare with the teaching example
Look for a welcome that invites honest reactions, a follow-up that uses the buyer’s answer, and a specific agreed plan. Feedback names an observed moment; the retry improves that moment. A decision to wait can be sound when the plan fits the reason.
slides.theme: tru alms day3-polish lesson lesson-photo photo-practice
slides.notes:
Use rotating trios with agent, buyer, and observer, or pairs where the buyer gives feedback. In pairs, both take an agent turn and use the third round to retry the harder moment. In each turn briefly welcome the buyer, then move to the end of the fictional tour and build a plan from the card. Buyer: supply the card facts naturally when asked, and do not agree automatically. Observer: name one actual moment and one correction. Do not label a peer or self-check as coach sign-off. Submit the buyer answer and plan after the conversation, not before the buyer has spoken. If testing solo, set up solo speaking practice and record test observations. A solo run cannot verify a live peer’s performance.
Handoff: Bring back the plan your buyer actually agreed to. We’ll use that to check the follow-through.
Sources: R005–006; R020–025; INT-005–007,035–039,048–051. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Bring back the plan your buyer actually agreed to. We’ll use that to check the follow-through.

What plan did you agree on: purpose, actions, and next contact?

rubric.label: Uses the buyer’s answer in a relevant follow-up
Connects help to the buyer’s actual concern
Checks agreement on actions and next contact

slides.title: Would your next contact move the plan forward?
slides.lead: Use the buyer conversation you just practiced. Write the note and next task you would save, then explain the purpose of your next contact.
slides.body:
Partner check: Is the plan based on what the buyer said? Can someone tell who does what and when?

Compare with the teaching example
The note reflects the conversation, separates unknowns from facts, and records the agreed action. The stage matches the completed appointment. The task supports a useful next contact at the agreed time or trigger.
slides.notes:
Give a minute to write and submit. Read two contrasting plans with permission. Ask the room what each next contact will accomplish. Correct invented facts, missing agreement, or a generic “checking in.” Have the agent revise that part. This is a written practice record, not a change to a real FUB contact. Review the real submitted answers in the presenter panel.
Handoff: To close, let’s name what you should now be able to do at your next showing.
Sources: R021; INT-037–039. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: To close, let’s name what you should now be able to do at your next showing.

activity.prompt: Use the buyer conversation you just practiced. Write the note and next task you would save, then explain the purpose of your next contact.

fields.label: Write the factual note, correct stage, and next task. Include the reason for the next contact.

activity.model: The note reflects the conversation, separates unknowns from facts, and records the agreed action. The stage matches the completed appointment. The task supports a useful next contact at the agreed time or trigger.

slides.title: Your next showing should end with a plan
slides.lead: You should now be able to guide the visit from the first welcome through the next agreed step.
slides.body:
Conduct the showing

Prepare useful comparisons and make honest reactions welcome.

Understand the buyer

Follow their answers into priorities, concerns, and timing.

Build momentum

Recommend a useful next step, confirm the plan, and follow through.
slides.notes:
Ask two agents to name a behavior they will use at their next showing and why. Remind them that helping the buyer can include a better search, a lender conversation, getting an answer, or a thoughtful plan to wait. The worksheet has the question bank and practice cards. End the live session when ready; normal sessions create follow-up practice, while solo rehearsals create no real-agent assignments. Day 4 can build on the financing questions that surfaced today.
Handoff: Before your next showing, review the questions and choose one thing to practice. Afterward, check whether your buyer left with a plan they understood.
Sources: Eric’s Day 3 objective; R005; R020–025. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
slides.cue: Before your next showing, review the questions and choose one thing to practice. Afterward, check whether your buyer left with a plan they understood.

cases.name: Case 1 · The home does not fit
cases.quote: “We liked the living area, but I could hear everything from the office. We are still figuring out what matters.”
cases.goal: Buyer facts: one buyer takes work calls at home; a quiet enclosed office matters more than an extra bedroom. They want to compare two quieter layouts next Saturday if access works. Reveal the reason when asked. Agent: learn what “quiet” requires and agree on a search and confirmation plan; do not promise access.

cases.name: Case 2 · The timing has a reason
cases.quote: “We like the home, but we keep saying a year. I do not know what payment we would be comfortable with.”
cases.goal: Buyer facts: a year is an estimate, not a fixed deadline. They have not spoken to a lender and want information before deciding whether buying fits. They are open to an introduction, not committed to buying. Agent: clarify the concern, offer relevant preparation, and agree how to reconnect without accelerating their decision.

cases.name: Case 3 · An answer is holding up the decision
cases.quote: “This one could work, but the roof worries me. I need to understand that before deciding whether to take the next step.”
cases.goal: Buyer facts: the roof age is unknown. They would like to consider an offer soon if they can understand the issue, but have not decided to offer. They can talk again at six. Agent: establish what information matters and how urgent it is, seek appropriate help, and agree on an update without promising the outside answer.

resources: Use the question bank and buyer cards to practice again. In a live session, submit your responses through your learner screen. The printed worksheet does not submit answers. Keep practice evidence separate from observed work with an actual client.
